canonical_answers: Continuity gives 8.00 m/s in the narrow section; Bernoulli predicts lower static pressure there.

payload.text: Water flows steadily from a 4.00 cm² section of a horizontal pipe at 2.00 m/s into a 1.00 cm² section.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Predict how the observable changes when the defining scale parameter is doubled, and justify the prediction quantitatively.

criteria.description: Doubling the narrow section's cross-sectional area (from 1.00 cm² to 2.00 cm²) halves the exit speed to 4.00 m/s, since continuity gives v2 = A1v1/A2, which is inversely proportional to A2; because the speed difference between sections shrinks, Bernoulli's equation predicts a smaller pressure drop in the narrow section.
required_evidence: exit speed halves to 4.00 m/s because v2 is inversely proportional to A2
pressure drop becomes smaller because the speed difference between sections shrinks
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.
criteria.minimum_fix: To earn this point, explicitly show exit speed halves to 4.00 m/s because v2 is inversely proportional to A2; pressure drop becomes smaller because the speed difference between sections shrinks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why assuming the water is incompressible and the flow steady lets you apply continuity (A1v1 = A2v2) and Bernoulli's equation to justify the higher speed and lower pressure in the narrow section.

criteria.description: Correctly cites the continuity equation and Bernoulli's principle as the governing relations and states that the flow is assumed steady and the water incompressible.
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.
criteria.minimum_fix: To earn this point, explicitly show incompressible, steady flow; Bernoulli relates speed and pressure.
